title: California’s new tyre standard is stricter than Europe’s, which has had one since 2012
summary:
California’s Energy Commission has unanimously approved the first US efficiency standard for replacement tyres, capping rolling resistance from 2029 and tightening it in 2033.
Its Energy Commission voted unanimously on Monday to cap rolling resistance on replacement tyres from 2029, tightening the limit again in 2033.
Europe has enforced a rolling resistance ceiling since 2012 under UN Regulation 117, currently 10.5 newtons per kilonewton for passenger car tyres.
Every tyre sold in the EU has carried a label since 2012 grading rolling resistance, wet grip and noise, sitting next to the price, and no American equivalent was ever adopted.
Tyre makers estimate around 70% of the current market would fail, while California’s own regulatory analysis found that between 82% and 91% of replacement tyres would not comply at the second threshold.

title: China’s solar power rollout is harming birds, a new analysis finds
summary:
A new analysis studied the solar policies and bird diversity in more than 2300 counties across China.
China is the world leader in solar power, but the country’s massive boom in this clean energy source could have unintended consequences for the country’s birds.
Using birdwatching and policy data from more than 2,300 counties across China, a new analysis found that areas with stricter policies enforcing solar energy development have seen decreases in bird diversity over the last 10 years.
Constructing solar power plants can affect the vegetation and landscape around them—including the creatures that live there.
That said, the analysis is the first he has seen that has looked at the relationship between solar policy and biodiversity on a national level.

title: Trump admin moves to allow logging and construction in national forests
summary:
For 25 years, the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, commonly called the “Roadless Rule”, established broad prohibitions on road construction and timber harvesting on nearly 45 million acres of National Forest System lands.
However, the Trump administration announced this week that it is moving ahead with plans to rescind the 2001 rule that blocked road construction, logging and other development on national forest lands, saying the “one-size-fits-all restriction” has frustrated land managers and served as a barrier to reducing wildfire risk across the nation’s national forests.
The proposed rule would not apply to national forests in Colorado and Idaho, where separate state-specific roadless regulations are in place.
“For 25 years, the Roadless Rule has tied the hands of local land managers with a one-size-fits-all federal policy.
The public will have an opportunity to comment on the proposed rule and draft environmental statement before it becomes final.

title: Photos: Releasing Animals Back Into Their Habitats
summary:
Maria Derhachova / Global Images Ukraine / GettyAn employee of the Ukrainian Bat Center holds a bat in her hand while preparing it for flight on April 5, 2026, in Lviv, Ukraine.
All bat species found in Ukraine have the status of “vulnerable” or “rare” and are listed in the Red Book of Ukraine.
During the winter, volunteers care for bats that could not find a place for hibernation or are injured.
They are fed, treated, and sent into hibernation.
In spring, they are released into the natural environment so that they can continue their life in usual conditions.

summary:
Keith Elias's family have been fishing on the river for 300 years - he said he had only caught one fish this season.
Last year, the nearby River Teifi had been noted as one of the UK's most polluted rivers, with 2,232 spills lasting more than 22,000 hours recorded in 2024.
It has been reported that some incidents of pollution were made by Welsh Water.
The company said it would invest £889m on storm overflows between 2025 and 2030, including six projects to reduce their impact on the Tywi.
Local people have also shared videos online of discharge across the river, which they claim appear to be from a nearby electronics recycling company Mekatek.

title: Giant whales move into Greenland waters as ice disappears
summary:
Sea ice has been disappearing from East Greenland, allowing giant whales to take advantage and move into previously inaccessible areas.
That is the conclusion of a decades-long study that has recorded - and filmed - hundreds of the world's biggest whales including humpbacks, minke and fin whales, feeding in ice-free seas along the coast in summer.
None of these marine mammals were historically found here as they have been locked out of the coastal waters by ice.
Now, as climate change warms the sea and melts that ice, they have adapted.
Scientists describe the result as seasonal Arctic "feeding frenzies" - part of a major regime shift in the ocean environment along East Greenland.
